finding.claim: Negative amount on /transfer lets the sender take money from any existing account. No amount sign check, so the overdraft test passes and the debit becomes a credit.

finding.guards_checked: bank.py:11 overdraft check only; no amount>0 check on /transfer (contrast /withdraw bank.py:21 which has amount<=0). No recipient existence or ownership check on 'to'.

verdict.guard_found: Only the overdraft check at bank.py:11 (BAL[g.user] < amount). For a negative amount it is false, so it never aborts. /transfer has no amount>0 check (the /withdraw check at bank.py:21 is absent here). No check on 'to' beyond the KeyError from BAL[to] at bank.py:14, which only means the recipient must already exist.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches bank.py:9-14: the overdraft check at line 11 cannot fire for a negative amount, so BAL[g.user] -= amount (line 13) raises the sender's balance and BAL[to] += amount (line 14) lowers the existing victim's balance. The attacker is any caller whose identity sets g.user; that assignment is not in this repo (only bank.py exists), so the attacker level is assumed to be an ordinary authenticated user, which is the exposure the claim describes.

finding.claim: Non-finite amount (NaN, Infinity, -Infinity, accepted by Python json) passes both endpoints' checks. NaN makes the balance NaN, after which every overdraft comparison is false and the account can spend without limit. -Infinity gives the same effect as F1.
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] -= amount (bank.py:13, bank.py:23) and BAL[to] += amount (bank.py:14)

finding.guards_checked: bank.py:11 and bank.py:21 only reject finite negative/overdraft cases; NaN and Infinity comparisons evaluate false and pass. No math.isfinite or isinstance checks anywhere.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only checks are bank.py:11 (`BAL[g.user] < amount` → abort) and bank.py:21 (`amount <= 0 or BAL[g.user] < amount` → abort). For NaN both comparisons are false, so neither aborts. Infinity/-Infinity are not rejected either. No isfinite/isinstance check exists anywhere, and Flask's request.json uses Python's json module, which accepts NaN/Infinity by default.
verdict.reason: bank.py:10 takes `amount` from request.json with no finiteness check, and bank.py:11 and bank.py:21 compare with `<`/`<=` so NaN passes; bank.py:13 and bank.py:23 then set the balance to NaN, after which every overdraft comparison is false and withdrawals are unlimited. The attacker needs only a session that sets g.user, which is set outside this file (the only file in the directory, so the auth layer isn't visible here), so it is any account holder, not a privileged role.

finding.claim: Check-then-act race: balance check and debit are not atomic, so concurrent requests can both pass the overdraft check and overdraw the account (double spend).
finding.source: Concurrent POST /withdraw (bank.py:18-20) and POST /transfer (bank.py:7-10) requests for the same user

trace.note: request A reads BAL[g.user] >= amount and passes
request B reads the same balance and passes before A debits
A debits, then B debits; balance goes below zero

finding.guards_checked: No lock, transaction or atomic compare-and-swap around check and debit. Depends on the server running requests concurrently (Flask dev server is threaded by default; production server config is not in the repo and was not checked).

verdict.guard_found: none. The balance check and debit have no lock, transaction, or atomic operation: bank.py:11-13 (transfer) and bank.py:21-23 (withdraw) are a plain read, compare, then `-=`. The only check is the `abort(400)` on the overdraft comparison, and that check is the racy one. The candidate's line references all match the file: source lines 7-10 and 18-20, check lines 11 and 21, debit lines 13 and 23.
verdict.reason: bank.py:21-23 (and bank.py:11-13) read BAL[g.user] and compare it to amount, then subtract with no lock or atomic step, so concurrent requests from the same user can both pass the check and overdraw the balance (bank.py:23). Caveat: g.user is set outside this file, and the race only exists if the production server handles requests concurrently. The Flask dev server is threaded by default, and the production server configuration is not in the repo.

finding.claim: UNCERTAIN: no authentication in the repo. g.user, which keys every balance read and write, is never assigned here. Standalone, both endpoints raise AttributeError (500). If an external layer sets g.user from client-controlled input, any caller controls any account.
finding.source: Every route in bank.py (/transfer bank.py:7, /withdraw bank.py:18); identity expected in g.user

verdict.guard_found: none. No auth decorator, before_request hook, or g.user assignment exists in the repo (only bank.py is present). The only input-validation control is the amount check on /withdraw at bank.py:21 (amount <= 0), which does not constrain the identity key.
verdict.reason: All four cited lines (bank.py:11, 13, 21, 23) exist and do what the trace says, but whether any caller can control g.user depends on an external layer that is not in the repo; nothing in bank.py:7-24 sets g.user from client input (request.json supplies only "to" and "amount"), so the cross-account impact cannot be confirmed or refuted from this code. Side note, outside the candidate's claim: /transfer (bank.py:10, 11, 13-14) has no amount > 0 check, so an authenticated user could send a negative amount to drain another account, which is a separate issue worth its own finding.
